newsitem.title: FRANCE: Council of Europe suspends Belarus guest status.
newsitem.headline: Council of Europe suspends Belarus guest status.

text.p: The Council of Europe, the pan-European body which promotes democracy and human rights, decided on Monday to suspend Belarus's special guest status, saying its new legislature had no democratic legitimacy.

Leni Fischer, president of the 40-nation Council's parliamentary assembly, said it took the decision because the former Soviet republic's new constitution did not respect minimum democratic standards.
"Belarus's new constitution is illegal, and...does not respect minimum democratic standards and violates the principles of separation of powers and the rule of law," Fischer said in a statement.

She said the assembly could not accept continued relations with a parliament appointed by President Alexander Lukashenko after a bitterly disputed November referendum which increased his powers and extended his term beyond the year 2000.
"We nevertheless preferred suspension to withdrawal of guest status from Belarus so as to maintain contact and support positive developments," Fischer said.

The decision was taken on the day President Boris Yeltsin raised the possibility of a merger between Russia and Belarus, saying in a letter to an enthusiastic Lukashenko that the two states should consider a referendum over unification "in one form or another."

The two Slav states signed an accord last April on closer economic and political ties and formed a loose community. Analysts said the Yeltsin letter was a sign of Russian anger over NATO's moves to expand eastwards to take in former Communist Central European states.

The special guest status was introduced in 1989 as a half-way house for former Communist bloc states which wished to join the Strasbourg-based Council, often regarded as an antechamber to membership of the European Union.

Belarus was granted special guest status in September 1992, allowing a seven-member parliamentary delegation to attend sessions of the assembly in recognition of Minsk's move towards democracy and respect for human rights.
However, the Council repeatedly warned Lukashenko against going ahead with the disputed referendum, which it declared to have only consultative value.

Fischer recalled that the Council's so-called Venice Commission of independent constitutional experts had found that the draft constitution proposed by Lukashenko fell short of minimum democratic standards.
